one_liner: Go goroutines passing a token round a 503-member ring, 2.4x faster than a C++ Boost.Asio program on 503 OS threads.
what_it_does: This entry is the Go language runtime (goroutines plus sync primitives), measured on the Benchmarks Game thread-ring task in the SCOOP/Qs paper (West, Nanz, Meyer). The Go program starts 503 goroutines, each holding a sync.Mutex used as a binary semaphore; a hand-off writes the next member's counter, unlocks its mutex and calls runtime.Gosched(). It is not a library and not a drop-in for anything in C++: to get the effect you write the service in Go.
how_it_is_fast: A hand-off never leaves user space in the common case: Mutex.Unlock on a parked waiter calls the runtime semaphore release, which readies the waiting goroutine on the current P (runtime.ready puts it in the run queue), and Gosched puts the current goroutine on the global queue and runs the next one on the same OS thread. The C++ baseline instead posts each pass to one shared boost::asio::io_service queue; in Boost 1.55 every post() takes the io_service mutex and signals an idle OS thread's wakeup event (task_io_service::wake_one_thread_and_unlock), so each pass is a kernel-level wake-up and context switch among 503 pthreads. The win is M:N user-space scheduling against 1:1 OS threads, not code generation.
when_to_use: Services built from thousands of mostly-blocked tasks that hand work to each other in sequence (pipelines, actor-like rings), where a C++ design would otherwise park one OS thread per task.
Choosing a language for a new concurrent service when the C++ alternative under consideration is thread-per-task rather than coroutines or fibers.
Message-passing code where cheap goroutine creation (503 here, millions in practice) matters more than peak single-thread speed.
when_not_to_use: As evidence that Go beats C++ in general: the paper's own geometric mean over its concurrent tasks ranks C++/TBB first (1.57 s) ahead of Go (1.82 s); thread-ring and condition are the stated exceptions because both are essentially single-threaded (search snippet).

When a C++ fiber or coroutine runtime (Boost.Fiber, Boost.Context, C++20 coroutines) or a single-threaded loop is an option: none was measured, and those remove the OS-thread wake-up that the baseline pays on every pass.
When you need the fastest runtime for this pattern: Erlang processes did the same ring in 3.30 s against Go's 13.98 s in the same table.
Inside an existing C++ program: calling Go goes through cgo or a separate process, and Go brings a garbage collector and its own scheduler.

integration.dependencies: Go toolchain and runtime (no third-party packages; the benchmark uses only fmt, os, runtime, strconv, sync)
integration.min_toolchain: Not stated by the paper or repo; code dates from 2014 (Go 1.2/1.3 era) and uses only APIs still present in current Go
integration.thread_safety: sync.Mutex is documented as not tied to a goroutine (one goroutine may lock, another unlock), which the benchmark relies on; Unlock synchronizes-before the next Lock per the Go memory model

gotchas: Harness asymmetry: run_all.py passes the worker count as $2, and only the Go run.sh uses it (GOMAXPROCS=$2). The C++ program ignores its second argument and always runs 503 OS threads on every core, and Erlang's run.sh sets no +S, so it uses all schedulers. The concurrent tasks run with worker_range = [4] at HEAD, and the search snippet ties the paper's '32 cores' label to Figure 18 (parallel tasks), so Table 5 may be GOMAXPROCS=4 rather than 32.

The baseline's '4 KB stacks' never took effect on Linux: glibc's pthread_attr_setstack returns EINVAL below PTHREAD_STACK_MIN (check_stacksize_attr in glibc 2.19; 16384 bytes on x86-64), main.cpp ignores the return value, and the 503 threads were created with default-size stacks. This does not change the timing much, but the record's baseline description is wrong on this point.

Each language was run once (range(0, 1)) and timed as wall clock around Popen, so process start and creating 503 pthreads count against C++. Erlang alone reports its own timer:tc figure, which excludes VM boot.

Not reproducible as published against current Boost: main.cpp uses asio::io_service and io_service::post(), and boostorg/asio develop (Asio 1.38.2) has neither the io_service typedef nor an io_context::post member, so it needs a port to io_context and asio::post() before it builds.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this over the GHC skynet entry when the question is hand-off latency between long-lived tasks rather than spawn cost. Pick Erlang's thread-ring entry, from the same paper, if the fastest runtime for this pattern matters (3.30 s against Go's 13.98 s). Pick the luncliff Comparison-Go-CppTBB entry when the C++ alternative is a real TBB task scheduler, because this entry's 'TBB' column is Boost.Asio over OS threads.
verified_claims_summary: WebSearch summaries of Table 5 in arXiv 1405.7153 give 13.98 s for Go and 34.13 s for the 'C++/TBB' column on thread-ring (503 members, 5,000,000 passes), about 2.4x. The C++ program is the Benchmarks Game Boost.Asio version over 503 pthreads, built with g++ -O3. Compiler and runtime versions, the CPU model and the effective GOMAXPROCS of the published run are not stated anywhere opened.
status_note: Go is active and BSD-3-Clause licensed (139.2k stars); the evidence is a single-run 2014 academic comparison whose paper could not be opened (snippet only), whose C++ side no longer builds against current Boost.Asio, and whose worker setting constrained only the Go run, so treat the 2.4x as directional for goroutines against OS threads.
